problem:
Which of the following augmented matrices are in row echelon form?

Select all that apply.
solution:
Remember that an augmented matrix is in row echelon form if its coefficient matrix satisfies the following conditions:

- All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the bottom of the matrix.
- Each leading entry of a row is in a column to the right of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

- The matrix $A$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
A=\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}2 & 3 & -7 & 1 \\ 0 & 4 & 3 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 5\end{array}\right]
$$

- The matrix $B$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
B=\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}3 & 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]
$$

- The matrix $C$ is not in row echelon form since ${c}_{22}\ne 0$ (condition II is violated).

$$
C=\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -4 & 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 3 & 2\end{array}\right]
$$

Therefore, only $A$ and $B$ are in row echelon form.

problem:
Given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x) & ={\begin{aligned}5x-5, & x<1 \\ 0, & x=1 \\ {x}^{3}-1, & x>1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
solution:
Let's check our continuity conditions:

- $g(1)=0$ exists $\,✓$

- The left and right-sided limits are

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{-}}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{-}}(5x-5)=5(1)-5=0, \\ {lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{+}}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{+}}({x}^{3}-1)={1}^{3}-1=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the left and right-sided limits are equal, we conclude that statement ${lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}g(x)={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}g(x)$ is true and

$$
{lim}_{x\to 1}g(x)=0.\,\,✓
$$

- The value of the limit is ${lim}_{x\to 1}g(x)=0,$ and the value of the function is $g(1)=0.$ So, statement ${lim}_{x\to 1}g(x)=g(1)$ is true and

$$
{lim}_{x\to 1}g(x)=g(1)\,\,✓
$$

So, the function is continuous at $x=0,$ and statement “$g(x)$ has a removable discontinuity at $x=1$” is false.

In conclusion, only statements ${lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}g(x)={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}g(x)$ and ${lim}_{x\to 1}g(x)=g(1)$ are true.

problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the finite region bounded between the parabola $y=1-{x}^{2}$ and the line $y=-3?$

Select all that apply.
solution:
First, notice that

$$
y=1-{x}^{2}\,⟹\,x=\pm \sqrt{1-y}.
$$

Now, let's sketch our region.

![](images/72/726ad8599b89029d3dba8e79ca947af99c17bd8712e551e49fc33d3e597a5cb7.png)

We have the following:

- Any vertical line through the region intersects it on a single interval. Furthermore, we can represent our region as

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 2,\,-3\le y\le 1-{x}^{2}\}.
$$

So, this is a type I region.

- Any horizontal line through the region intersects it on a single interval. Furthermore, we can represent our region as

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-3\le y\le 1,\,-\sqrt{1-y}\le x\le \sqrt{1-y}\}.
$$

So, this is a type II region.

Therefore, only statements “It is a type I region” and “It is a type II region” are true.

problem:
Which of the following equalities are true given that
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,1\le y\le 3\}.$

Select all that apply.
solution:
We notice that:

- the limits for the variable $x$ are from $0$ to $1$, and

- the limits for the variable $y$ are from $1$ to $3.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{1}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{1}y\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the region of integration is rectangular, we can simply swap the order of integration. This gives

$$
{∬}_{D}y\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}A={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{1}^{3}y\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x.
$$

So, the correct answer is ${∬}_{D}y\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}A={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{3}y\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x$ only.

problem:
Consider the following set of polynomials:

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=2t,\,{p}_{2}(t)=t+1,\,{p}_{3}(t)=2t+1.
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space ${R}_{1}[t]$ of polynomials of degree at most $1$ in the variable $t$ is defined as 

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(0)q(0)+p(-1)q(-1),
$$

which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
solution:
Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement “${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨2t,t+1⟩ \\  & =(2t){|}_{0}\cdot (t+1){|}_{0}+(2t){|}_{-1}\cdot (t+1){|}_{-1} \\  & =2(0)\cdot (0+1)+2(-1)\cdot ((-1)+1) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement “${p}_{1}(t)⊥̸{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” is true since

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨2t,2t+1⟩ \\  & =(2t){|}_{0}\cdot (2t+1){|}_{0}+(2t){|}_{-1}\cdot (2t+1){|}_{-1} \\  & =2(0)\cdot (2(0)+1)+2(-1)\cdot (2(-1)+1) \\  & =2\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥̸{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement “$S=\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product” is false. Since ${p}_{1}(t)⊥̸{p}_{3}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is “${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product”; “${p}_{1}(t)⊥̸{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” only.

problem:
![](images/34/3411e11060b06a11c82ad677f50731faa31c6bc2e83ccb0d0d10931cf3d76592.png)

Consider the vector field $F$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true everywhere in the domain of $F?$

Select all that apply.
solution:
Recall that $\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F$ denotes the divergence of the vector field $F.$

Intuitively, the divergence of $F$ at a point $P$ measures how much $F$ acts like a source or a sink at $P:$

- If $∇\cdot F>0$ at $P,$ then $F$ acts like a source at $P.$

- If $∇\cdot F<0$ at $P,$ then $F$ acts like a sink at $P.$

- If $∇\cdot F=0$ at $P,$ then $F$ acts like neither a source nor a sink at $P.$

![](images/6c/6c747149618d4c5ef35e727af15cd001365bd9c2d5e064689baf24c6ee23cff9.png)

If $∇\cdot F=0$ everywhere in the domain of $F,$ we say that $F$ is solenoidal.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statement $\text{div}\,F<0$ is true, whereas statements $\text{div}\,F=0$ and $\text{div}\,F>0$ are false. Notice that the lengths of the vectors decrease as we move in the $y$-direction. Therefore, the vector field $F$ acts like a sink at every point.

- Statement “$F$ is solenoidal” is false. Since $∇\cdot F\ne 0,$ the vector field $F$ is not solenoidal.

Therefore, the correct answer is $\text{div}\,F<0$ only.

problem:
![](images/38/38a7ae83a66a2c1ff6a012b9405c6621b0c0a162018065549e75a1d08bc04d44.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z),$ shown above. Given that $F(x,y,z)$ is independent of $z,$ which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
solution:
Recall that $\text{curl}\,F$ denotes the curl of the vector field $F.$

To understand intuitively whether a vector field has curl at a point $P$, imagine that our vector field $F$ represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water. We place a paddlewheel at $P$ with the axis of rotation pointing in the $z$-direction, and we note whether the paddlewheel rotates or not.

- If the paddlewheel does not rotate due to the action of the water, then the velocity field has zero curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F=0.$

- If the paddlewheel is forced to rotate due to the action of the water, then the vector field has curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0.$

![](images/59/594106633e422d24b9fea113d24fb6367fdef5ac52724931860e4163e33ce992.png)

Moreover, if $\text{curl}\,F=0$ everywhere in ${R}^{3}$, we say that $F$ is irrotational.

With that in mind, let's check each statement:

- Statement $\text{curl}\,F=0$ is true, whereas statement $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0$ is false. If a paddlewheel were placed at any point $P$ in the manner described above, it would not rotate. Therefore, $\text{curl}\,F=0.$

- Statements “$F$ is irrotational” is true. Since $\text{curl}\,F=0,$ the vector field $F$ is irrotational.

- Statement “$\text{curl}\,F$ points in the negative $z$-direction” is false. Since $\text{curl}\,F=0,$ it points in neither the positive nor the negative $z$-direction.

Therefore, the correct answer is $\text{curl}\,F=0$; “$F$ is irrotational” only.

problem:
Which of the following subspaces must be orthogonal to $\text{Null}(A)$ for every matrix $A?$

Select all that apply.
solution:
Recall that $\text{Null}(A)$ contains all vectors that, when pre-multiplied by $A,$ result in the zero-vector $0.$ 

When pre-multiplying a vector by $A,$ we actually multiply each row of $A$ by that vector. So, $\text{Null}(A)$ must be orthogonal to the row space of $A,$ which is $\text{Col}({A}^{T}).$

problem:
Let $C$ be a simple, piecewise-smooth, closed, and positively oriented curve. Given that the line integral

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y
$$

represents the area of the region $D$ enclosed by any such curve in ${R}^{2},$ which of the following could be the functions $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y)?$

Select all that apply.
solution:
According to Green's theorem, if 

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,
$$

we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

With that in mind, let's examine each pair in turn.

- Pair “$P(x,y)=y$ and $Q(x,y)=-x$” does *not* give the required area. In this case, 
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-1,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2\ne 1.
$$

- Pair “$P(x,y)=\frac{x}{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=\frac{y}{2}$” does *not* give the required area. Notice that
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2y\operatorname{sin}⁡{y}^{2}$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=0,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y\operatorname{sin}⁡{y}^{2}\ne 1.
$$

- Pair “$P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x$” gives the required area. Notice that
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is “$P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x$” only.

problem:
Let $C$ be a simple, piecewise-smooth, closed, and positively oriented curve. Given that the line integral

$$

$$

represents the area of the region $D$ enclosed by any such curve in ${R}^{2},$ which of the following could be the vector field $F(x,y)?$

solution:
According to Green's theorem, if $F(x,y)=⟨P(x,y),\,Q(x,y)⟩,$ where

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,
$$

we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y \\  & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r\end{aligned}
$$

  

With that in mind, let's examine each pair in turn.

- Vector field $F(x,y)=⟨-y,\,{x}^{2}+x⟩$ does *not* give the required area. In this case, 
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-1$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2x+1,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2x+2\ne 1.
$$

- Vector field $F(x,y)=⟨-\frac{y}{4}+x,\,\frac{3x}{4}⟩$ gives the required area. Notice that
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{4}$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\frac{3}{4},$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1.
$$

- Vector field $F(x,y)=⟨-y,\,0⟩$ gives the required area. Notice that
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-1$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=0,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $F(x,y)=⟨-\frac{y}{4}+x,\,\frac{3x}{4}⟩$; $F(x,y)=⟨-y,\,0⟩$ only.

problem:
The region $R$ is bounded between the elliptic paraboloid $y={x}^{2}+{z}^{2}$ and the plane $y=2x.$ Given its representation 

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,{f}_{1}(x,z)\le y\le {f}_{2}(x,z)}
$$

as a type III region in three-dimensional space, which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
solution:
A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](images/c3/c3333ded3e00e7d7408f0dbd37807f1adec0301691cc6311871bfea6d7b9fa15.png)

 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement $D={(x,z)\,:\,(x-1)^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 1}$ is true, while statement $D={(x,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 2}$ is false. First, we find the projection of the intersection between the elliptic paraboloid $y={x}^{2}+{z}^{2}$ and the plane $y=2x$ onto $xz$-plane.

Notice that the equation of the plane is already solved for $y.$ Substituting this expression for $y$ into the equation of the paraboloid, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & ={x}^{2}+{z}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}-2x+{z}^{2} & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}-2x+1)+{z}^{2} & =1 \\ (x-1)^{2}+{z}^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 
So, the projection of the intersection is the circle $(x-1)^{2}+{z}^{2}=1$ centered at $(1,0)$ in the $xz$-plane. Hence, the domain $D$ is given by the following disc:

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,(x-1)^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 1}
$$

- Statement “${f}_{1}(x,z)=2x$ and ${f}_{2}(x,z)={x}^{2}+{z}^{2}$” is false. We have that $y$ is

- bounded *below* by ${f}_{1}(x,z)={x}^{2}+{z}^{2}$, and

- bounded *above* by ${f}_{2}(x,z)=2x.$

Therefore, the correct answer is $D={(x,z)\,:\,(x-1)^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 1}$ only.

problem:
The region $R$ is bounded between the elliptic paraboloid $x={y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$ and the plane $x=2y.$ Given its representation 

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,a\le y\le b,\,{g}_{1}(y)\le z\le {g}_{2}(y),\,{f}_{1}(y,z)\le x\le {f}_{2}(y,z)}
$$

as a type II region in three-dimensional space, which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
solution:
A typical three-dimensional region of type II can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](images/e4/e4c9cbbad2f13e9cc125ddbb89125ed2d734eee3f80737125961f4af1846a972.png)

 

Let's find a type II representation of our region.

**Step 1.** We start by finding the surfaces ${f}_{1}(y,z)$ and ${f}_{2}(y,z).$ Since all $x$ in the region are bounded *below* by $x={y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$ and *above* by $x=2y,$ we have

$$
\underbrace{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}_{{f}_{1}(y,z)}\le x\le \underbrace{2y}_{{f}_{2}(y,z)}.
$$

So, statement “${f}_{1}(y,z)={y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$ and ${f}_{2}(y,z)=2y$” is true.

**Step 2.** We find the projection of the intersection between the elliptic paraboloid $x={y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$ and the plane $x=2y$ onto the $yz$-plane.

Notice that the equation of the plane is already solved for $x.$ Substituting this expression for $x$ into the equation of the paraboloid, we obtain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}2y & ={y}^{2}+{z}^{2} \\ {y}^{2}-2y+{z}^{2} & =0 \\ ({y}^{2}-2y+1)+{z}^{2} & =1 \\ (y-1)^{2}+{z}^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =uv{|}_{-\pi }^{\pi }-{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{u}^{′}v\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t){|}_{-\pi }^{\pi }+{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(-\pi ))+\operatorname{sin}⁡t{|}_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\  & =(\pi +\pi )+(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )) \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}

Recall that a matrix $Q$ is orthogonal if and only if

$$
Q{Q}^{T}={Q}^{T}Q=I.
$$

To check that a matrix is orthogonal, it is sufficient to check that the above equation is satisfied.

Moreover, we have the following properties:

- For any orthogonal matrix $Q,$ we have ${Q}^{-1}={Q}^{T}.$

- $(AB)^{T}={B}^{T}{A}^{T}$ for conformable matrices $A$ and $B.$

With that in mind, let's inspect each of the statements in turn.

- Statement “${Q}^{T}$ is orthogonal” is true. Computing the product ${Q}^{T}\cdot ({Q}^{T})^{T},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}^{T}\cdot ({Q}^{T})^{T} & ={Q}^{T}Q \\  & =I.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “The identity matrix $I$ is orthogonal” is true. The columns of the identity matrix are orthonormal. Therefore, $I$ is an orthogonal matrix.

- Statement “$2Q$ is orthogonal” is false. Computing the product $2Q\cdot (2Q)^{T},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2Q\cdot (2Q)^{T} & =2Q\cdot 2{Q}^{T} \\  & =4Q{Q}^{T} \\  & =4I \\  & \ne I.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is “${Q}^{T}$ is orthogonal”; “The identity matrix $I$ is orthogonal” only.

problem:
Consider the standard Hermitian inner product $⟨\,\cdot \,,\,\cdot \,⟩$ over $C.$ 
Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
solution:
Recall that the standard Hermitian inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties:

- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨\alpha a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$

- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\overset{―}{\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$

- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$

- It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement “$⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$” is true. Indeed, the inner product over $C$ has conjugate symmetry.

- Statement “$⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C$” is false. To factor out a constant multiple from the second argument, we must change it to its complex conjugate.

- Statement “$⟨a,b⟩\in R$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$” is false. The inner product over $C$ is a complex number in general.

Therefore, the correct answer is “$⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$” only.

problem:
Consider the following set of polynomials:

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=t,\,{p}_{2}(t)=t-1,\,{p}_{3}(t)=2t-2.
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space ${R}_{1}[t]$ of polynomials of degree at most $1$ in the variable $t$ is defined as 

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1),
$$

which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
solution:
Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement “${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨t,t-1⟩ \\  & =(t){|}_{0}\cdot (t-1){|}_{0}+(t){|}_{1}\cdot (t-1){|}_{1} \\  & =0\cdot (0-1)+1\cdot (1-1) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement “${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨t,2t-2⟩ \\  & =(t){|}_{0}\cdot (2t-2){|}_{0}+(t){|}_{1}\cdot (2t-2){|}_{1} \\  & =0\cdot (2(0)-2)+1\cdot (2(1)-2) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement “$S=\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product” is false. Let's check if ${p}_{2}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t).$ Computing the inner product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨t-1,2t-2⟩ \\  & =(t-1){|}_{0}\cdot (2t-2){|}_{0}+(t-1){|}_{1}\cdot (2t-2){|}_{1} \\  & =(0-1)\cdot (2(0)-2)+(1-1)\cdot (2(1)-2) \\  & =2\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{2}(t)⊥̸{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product. So, $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is “${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product”; “${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” only.

$$

$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

problem:
Consider the following differential equation:

$$
P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+4{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y=0
$$

Given that the differential equation is exact, which of the following functions could be $P(x,y)?$

Select all that apply.
solution:
A differential equation of the form

$$
P(x,y)\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\text{d}y=0
$$

is exact if it passes the exactness test, i.e.,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}
$$

In our case, we're given $Q(x,y)=4{y}^{3}.$ 

First, let's differentiate $Q(x,y)$ with respect to $x:$

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(4{y}^{3})=0
$$

Now, let's apply $\frac{∂}{∂y}$ to each of the given options:

- First, we check $P(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+8.$ This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+8)=0=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $P(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+8$ gives an exact equation.

- Next, we check $P(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-2)=0=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $P(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-2$ gives an exact equation.

- Finally, we check $P(x,y)=2x+7:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+7)=0=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $P(x,y)=2x+7$ gives an exact equation.

problem:
A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. The position of the particle $y(t)$ at time $t$ is governed by the equation

$$
{y}^{″}+9y=10{e}^{-t}.
$$

Which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for $y(t)?$

Note that $A,$ $B,$ $R$ and $ϕ$ are constants.

Select all that apply.
solution:
The general solution to this equation is the sum of the complementary function and a particular solution.

First, we find the complementary solution ${y}_{c}(t),$ which is the solution to the simple harmonic motion equation ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=0.$
It can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t$

In our case

$$
{\omega }^{2}=9\,⟹\,\omega =3.
$$

Thus, we have:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡3t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡3t$

Next, we find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(t).$ The particular solution is of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\alpha {e}^{-t}.
$$

By substituting the particular solution into the differential equation and equating coefficients, we find that $\alpha =1.$ So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)={e}^{-t}.
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)+{e}^{-t}$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)+{e}^{-t}$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡3t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡3t+{e}^{-t}$

Only $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)+{e}^{-t}$ and $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡3t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡3t+{e}^{-t}$ match the forms above. Therefore, the correct answer is $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)+{e}^{-t}$; $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡3t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡3t+{e}^{-t}$ only.

problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
solution:
Remember that, given the equation of a damped harmonic oscillator, the type of damping depends on the discriminant of the characteristic equation:

- $D>0$ leads to heavy damping,

- $D=0$ leads to critical damping, and

- $D<0$ leads to light damping.

With that in mind, let's inspect each equation.

- The differential equation ${y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}+2y$ represents the equation of damped harmonic motion. 
The auxiliary equation for $\lambda $ is

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +2=0.
$$

The discriminant of this quadratic equation is:

$$
\begin{aligned}D={2}^{2}-4(1)(2) & =-4<0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the given equation represents light damping, and so statement “${y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}+2y=0$ represents an oscillator undergoing light damping” is correct.

- The differential equation ${y}^{″}+10{y}^{′}+25y=0$ represents the equation of damped harmonic motion. 
The auxiliary equation for $\lambda $ is:

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+10\lambda +25=0.
$$

The discriminant of this quadratic equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}D={10}^{2}-4(1)(25) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the given equation represents critical damping, and so statement “${y}^{″}+10{y}^{′}+25y=0$ represents an oscillator undergoing critical damping” is correct.

- The differential equation ${y}^{″}+5{y}^{′}+3y$ represents the equation of damped harmonic motion. 
The auxiliary equation for $\lambda $ is:

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+5\lambda +3=0.
$$

The discriminant of this quadratic equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}D={5}^{2}-4(1)(3) & =13>0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the given equation represents heavy damping, and so statement “${y}^{″}+5{y}^{′}+3y=0$ represents an oscillator undergoing heavy damping” is correct.

In conclusion, the correct answer is “${y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}+2y=0$ represents an oscillator undergoing light damping”; “${y}^{″}+10{y}^{′}+25y=0$ represents an oscillator undergoing critical damping”; “${y}^{″}+5{y}^{′}+3y=0$ represents an oscillator undergoing heavy damping”.

Given the two planes $3x-y+z=0$ and $x-z+4=0$, which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
solution:
First, notice that:

- For the plane $3x-y+z=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨3,-1,1⟩.$

- For the plane $x-z+4=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Now, let's consider the statements.

- Statement “The cross product of the normal vectors of the planes is equal to $0.$” is false. Computing the cross product of the normal vectors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨3,-1,1⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 3 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =i+4j+k \\  & =⟨1,4,1⟩\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “The planes are parallel” is false. Since ${n}_{1}\times {n}_{2}\ne 0$, the vectors ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are not parallel. As a result, the planes are not parallel either.

- Statement “The planes intersect on a line” is true. Indeed, two non-parallel planes in $3$-dimensional space must intersect on a line.

Therefore, only statement “The planes intersect on a line” is true.

fields.key: The cross product of the normal vectors of the planes is equal to $0.$
The planes intersect on a line.

problem:
Given the two planes $-x-2y+z=0$ and $2x+4y-2z+1=0$, which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
solution:
First, notice that:

- For the plane $-x-2y+z=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨-1,-2,1⟩.$

- For the plane $2x+4y-2z+1=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨2,4,-2⟩.$

Now, let's consider the statements.

- Statement “The normal vectors of the planes are parallel” is true. Indeed, ${n}_{2}=-2{n}_{1}.$ So, the normal vectors are parallel.

- Statement “The planes are parallel but not coincident” is true, while statement “The planes are coincident” is false. 

For the two planes to coincide, the equation of one plane should be a scalar multiple of the other. However, if we try to manipulate the equation of the second plane to resemble the equation of the first plane, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+4y-2z+1=0 \\ x+2y-z+\frac{1}{2}=0 \\ -x-2y+z-\frac{1}{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Clearly, this equation is not the same as the equation of the first plane. So, the planes are parallel but not coincident.

Therefore, only statements “The normal vectors of the planes are parallel” and “The planes are parallel but not coincident” are true.

fields.key: The normal vectors of the planes are parallel.
The planes are parallel but not coincident.

problem:
![](images/d3/d3a06bdc7a63a86651752ff70331010920d24728e7f4e4ad9f067eb860ebaf4b.png)

Consider the phase line shown above. Which of the following differential equations could have this phase line?

Select all that apply.

If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
solution:
First, notice that all three differential equations are of the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y).
$$

The phase line gives us the following information:

- The equilibrium solutions are $y=-1$ and $y=1.$

- $f(y)$ is positive for $y\in (-\infty ,-1)\cup (1,\infty ).$

- $f(y)$ is negative for $y\in (-1,1).$

With this in mind, let's study each of the given equations.

- We start by considering ${y}^{′}={y}^{2}-1.$

First, we see that $f(y)={y}^{2}-1,$ so $f(y)=0$ if $y=-1,1.$ So, the equilibrium solutions correspond to those shown in the phase line.

Now, we can construct a sign table for $f(y)$ as follows: 

|  | $(-\infty ,-1)$ | $(-1,1)$ | $(1,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $y+1$ | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $y-1$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ |
| $f(y)$ | $+$ | $-$ | $+$ |

So, we have that $f(y)$ is negative for  $y\in (-1,1),$ and $f(y)$ is positive for $y\in (-\infty ,-1)\cup (1,\infty ).$ This corresponds to the arrows shown on the phase line.

Therefore, equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={y}^{2}-1$ has the given phase line.

- Next, we consider ${y}^{′}=(y-1)^{2}(y+1).$

First, $f(y)=(y-1)^{2}(y+1),$ so $f(y)=0$ if $y=-1,1.$ So, the equilibrium solutions correspond to those shown in the phase line.

However, we note that $f(y)<0$ for $y\in (-\infty ,-1).$ This does *not* correspond to the arrows shown on the phase line.

Therefore, equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=(y-1)^{2}(y+1)$ does not have the given phase line.

- Finally, we consider ${y}^{′}=(y-1)^{2}.$

In this case, $f(y)=(y-1)^{2},$ and the equilibrium solution is $y=1$ only.

Therefore, equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=(y-1)^{2}$ does not have the given phase line.

Therefore, the correct answer is $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={y}^{2}-1$ only.

A particular autonomous differential equation has the phase line shown above. Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
solution:
We can classify the equilibrium solutions of an autonomous ODE ${y}^{′}=f(y)$ by examining its phase line.

- An equilibrium solution is a *sink* if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line both point *toward* the equilibrium solution.

- An equilibrium solution is a *source* if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line both point *away* from the equilibrium solution.

- An equilibrium solution is a *node* if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line point in the same direction.

Let's check each statement:

- Statement “$y=-1$ is a source” is true. Notice that the arrow just above the point $y=-1$ points upward, and the arrow just below it points downward. In other words, both arrows point *away* from  $y=-1.$ This means that $y=-1$ is a source.

- Statement “$y=2$ is a sink” is true, while statement “$y=2$ is a node” is false. Notice that the arrow just above the point $y=2$ points downward, and the arrow just below it points upward. In other words, both arrows point *toward* the point $y=2.$This means that $y=2$ is a sink.

Therefore, the correct answer is “$y=-1$ is a source”; “$y=2$ is a sink” only.

$$

$$

Given the action of the matrices $A-2I$ and $A+3I$ on the nonzero vectors $u,v,w,x$ and $y$ as depicted above, which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
solution:
A *generalized eigenvector* ${v}_{n}$ of rank $n$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda $ of a matrix $A$ is a nonzero vector such that

$$
{v}_{n}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{n-1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }…\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }0,
$$

where ${v}_{n-1},{v}_{n-2},…,{v}_{1}\ne 0.$ An *eigenvector* is simply a generalized eigenvector of rank $1.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement “$w$ is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of $A$” is true. Indeed, since 

$$
w\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }0,
$$

i.e. $A-2I$ maps $w$ to $0$ in $1$ step, 
the vector $w$ is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of $A.$

- Statement “$u$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of $A$” is false. Since

$$
u\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }v\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }w\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }0,
$$

i.e. $A-2I$ maps $u$ to $0$ in $3$ steps, 
the vector $u$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $3,$ not $2.$

- Statement “$y$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $1$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-3$ of $A$” is true. Indeed, since

$$
y\overset{A+3I\,}{\to }0,
$$

i.e. $A+3I$ maps $y$ to $0$ in $1$ step, 
the vector $y$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $1$ (a.k.a. an eigenvector) corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-3$ of $A.$

Therefore, the correct answer is “$w$ is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of $A$”; “$y$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $1$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-3$ of $A$” only.

A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix},\,v=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
solution:
A *generalized eigenvector* ${v}_{2}$ of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda $ of a matrix $A$ is a nonzero vector such that

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }0,
$$

where ${v}_{1}\ne 0.$ Recall that an *eigenvector* is simply a generalized eigenvector of rank $1.$ 

With this in mind, let's examine our statements.

First, we compute $A-3I:$

$$
A-3I=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}
$$

- Next, we find the image of $v$ under the action of $A-3I:$

$$
(A-3I)v=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{w}\ne 0
$$

- Since we got a nonzero vector in the last step, we now compute the image of $w$ under the action of $A-3I:$

$$
(A-3I)w=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=0
$$

So, we obtain the following chain of maps:

$$
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{v}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{w}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{0}
$$

Here, we see that $A-3I$ maps $v$ to $0$ in $2$ steps.

Therefore:

$\,$ *$v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ of $A.$*

So, the correct answer is “$v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ of $A$” only.

problem:
$\,$ $P(x):$ $x-1<x.$

Given that the above predicate is defined over the universal set $Z,$ which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
solution:
The *universal quantification* of a predicate $P(x),$ defined over the universal set $U,$ transforms this predicate into a statement that we write as

$$
∀x\in U,\,P(x).
$$

This statement is true if the predicate $P(x)$ is true on the entire universal set $U,$ i.e. if the truth set ${T}_{P}$ of the predicate coincides with the universal set $U:$

$$
{T}_{P}=U
$$

First, we solve the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-1 & <x \\ -1 & <0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the final condition is true for all $x\in Z,$ we have that the truth set of our predicate is ${T}_{P}=Z.$

With that in mind, let's inspect each of the given statements.

- Statement “The truth set of $P(x)$ is $∅.$” is false. The truth set is *not* empty.

- Statement “The truth set of $P(x)$ is $Z.$” is true. Indeed, ${T}_{P}=Z.$

- Statement $∀x\in Z,\,P(x).$ is true. Since ${T}_{P}$ coincides with the universal set, the statement $∀x\in Z,\,P(x)$ is true.

Therefore, the correct answer is “The truth set of $P(x)$ is $Z.$”; $∀x\in Z,\,P(x).$ only.

problem:
$\,$ ${x}^{2}+2x-3=0$

Which of the following conditions are necessary for the above to be true?

Select all that apply.
solution:
Given that the implication $S⇒N$ is true, we have the following:

- $S$ being true *guarantees* that $N$ must also be true. Therefore, $S$ is a *sufficient condition* for $N.$

- For $S$ to be true, it is *necessary* that $N$ is true. Therefore, $N$ is a *necessary condition* for $S.$ However, note that $N$ being true does *not* guarantee that $S$ is true.

These ideas can be summarized as follows:

$$
\text{S}\text{ufficient}\,⇒\,\text{N}\text{ecessary}.
$$

  

In our case, we need to find the conditions that are *necessary* from the given one:

$$
({x}^{2}+2x-3=0)\,⇒\,\text{N}\text{ecessary}
$$

Note that the solution to the given equation is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2x-3 & =0 \\ (x+3)(x-1) & =0 \\ x & =-3,1\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's inspect each of the given conditions.

- Condition $x=1$ is *not* a necessary condition:

$$
({x}^{2}+2x-3=0)\,⇏\,(x=1)\,\,\times 
$$

For example, if $x=-3,$ then ${x}^{2}+2x-3=0,$ but $x\ne 1.$

- Condition $x<0$ is *not* a necessary condition:

$$
({x}^{2}+2x-3=0)\,⇏\,(x<0)\,\,\times 
$$

For example, if $x=1,$ then ${x}^{2}+2x-3=0,$ but $x≮0.$

- Condition $|x|<5$ is a necessary condition:

$$
({x}^{2}+2x-3=0)\,⇒\,(|x|<5)\,\,✓
$$

Each solution of ${x}^{2}+2x-3=0$ satisfies $|x|<5.$

Therefore, the correct answer is $|x|<5$ only.

problem:
Consider the following relation defined on the set $A$ containing all possible triangles in ${R}^{2}.$

$$
x\,R\,y\,⇔\,x≅y
$$

Recall that $x≅y$ means that $x$ and $y$ are congruent.

Which of the following are true?

Select all that apply.
solution:
Given a relation $R$ on a set $A$:

- $R$ is reflexive if and only if for all $x\in A,$ $x\,R\,x.$

- $R$ is symmetric if and only if for all $x,y\in A,$ if $x\,R\,y,$ then $y\,R\,x.$

- $R$ is transitive if and only if for all $x,y,z\in A,$ if $x\,R\,y$ and $y\,R\,z,$ then $x\,R\,z.$

If $R$ is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, then $R$ is an equivalence relation.

Let's consider each of the properties in turn.

- The relation $R$ is reflexive. For all $x\in A,$ we have $x≅x.$ Every triangle is congruent with itself.

- The relation $R$ is symmetric. For all $x,y\in A,$ if $x≅y,$ then $y≅x.$ To see why, note that if we can find a sequence of rigid motions in the plane that maps $x$ to $y$ (implying $x≅y),$ then we can always find a sequence of rigid motions that maps $y$ to $x.$

- The relation $R$ is transitive. For all $x,y,z\in A,$ if $x≅y,$ and $y≅z,$ then $x≅z.$ To see why, note that if we can find a sequence of rigid motions in the plane that maps $x$ to $y$ (implying $x≅y)$ and another sequence that maps $y$ to $z,$ then we can always find a sequence that maps $x$ to $z.$

- The relation $R$ is an equivalence relation since it's reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.

Therefore, the correct answer is “$R$ is reflexive”; “$R$ is symmetric”; “$R$ is transitive”; “$R$ is an equivalence relation”.

problem:
$$
{y}^{″}+y=0
$$

Consider the differential equation above. Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
solution:
Recall that to determine whether $y(x)$ is a solution to the differential equation, we substitute $y$ and its derivatives into the equation. 

Let's check each statement in turn.

- Statement “${y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)$ is a solution to the equation” is true. First, we find the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{1}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) \\ {y}_{1}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's substitute ${y}_{1}(x)$ and its derivatives into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) & =0 \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{1}(x)$ is a solution to the equation.

- Statement “${y}_{2}(x)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)$ is a solution to the equation” is true. First, we find the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{2}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′}(x) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) \\ {y}_{2}^{″}(x) & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's substitute ${y}_{2}(x)$ and its derivatives into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) & =0 \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{2}(x)$ is a solution to the equation.

- Statement “The functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ form a set of fundamental solutions to the equation” is false. Both ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions of the equation. To check if these functions are linearly independent, we compute the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) & 3\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(x) & 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(x) \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the  Wronskian equals $0$ for all $x\in R,$ the functions are not linearly independent. Hence, ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ don't form a set of fundamental solutions to the equation.

Therefore, the correct answer is “${y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)$ is a solution to the equation”; “${y}_{2}(x)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)$ is a solution to the equation” only.

${y}_{2}(x)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)$ is a solution to the equation.
The functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ form a set of fundamental solutions to the equation.

problem:
Which of the following functions are surjections?

solution:
A function $f:X\to Y$ is a **surjection** (also known as **onto**) if, for *every* element $y$ in $Y,$ there is at least one element in $X$ that maps to $y.$ 

Symbolically, we can write:

$f:X\to Y$ is a surjection if $∀\,y\in Y,$ $∃\,x\in X$ such that $f(x)=y.$

With this in mind, let's check each function.

- “$f:R\to (0,\infty )$ defined by $f(x)={3}^{x}$” is a surjection. Given $y\in (0,\infty ),$ choose $x={log}_{3}⁡y\in R.$ Then $f(x)=f({log}_{3}⁡y)={3}^{{log}_{3}⁡y}=y.$

- “$g:Q\to Q$ defined by $g(x)={x}^{2}$” is *not* a surjection. As a counterexample, choose $2\in Q.$ There is no number $x\in Q$ such that $g(x)=2.$ The only real solutions of $g(x)={x}^{2}=2$ are $x=\pm\sqrt{2}$, and neither belongs to $Q$.

- “$h:R\to R$ defined by $h(x)={x}^{2}$” is *not* a surjection. As a counterexample, choose $-1\in R.$ There is no number $x\in R$ such that $h(x)={x}^{2}=-1.$  In fact, ${x}^{2}\ge 0$ for all $x\in R$, with equality at $x=0$.

Therefore, the correct answer is “$f:R\to (0,\infty )$ defined by $f(x)={3}^{x}$” only.

- “$f:R\to R$ defined by $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$” is *not* a bijection because it is not surjective. Remember that the range of $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ is $[-1,1].$ This means that 

$$
-1\le \operatorname{cos}⁡x\le 1.
$$

So,  for example, there is no value $x\in R$ such that $f(x)=2.$

- “$g:Q\to Q$ defined by $g(x)={x}^{2}-2$” is *not* a bijection because it is not injective. For example, $1$ and $-1$ are distinct elements of $Q$, but $g(1)=-1=g(-1)$.

- “$h:Q\to Q$ defined by $h(x)=8x-3$” is a bijection. First of all, it is a surjection because $∀\,y\in Q,$ we can choose an $x\in Q$ such that $h(x)=y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}h(x) & =y \\ 8x-3 & =y \\ x & =\frac{y+3}{8}\in Q\end{aligned}
$$

We verify that, 

$$
h(x)=h(\frac{y+3}{8})=8(\frac{y+3}{8})-3=y.
$$

Second, it is an injection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}h({x}_{1}) & =h({x}_{2}) \\ 8{x}_{1}-3 & =8{x}_{2}-3 \\ {x}_{1} & ={x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Because $h$ is both surjective and injective, $h$ is bijective.

Therefore, the correct answer is “$h:Q\to Q$ defined by $h(x)=8x-3$” only.

problem:
Which of the following functions are surjections?

Select all that apply.
solution:
A function $f:X\to Y$ is a **surjection** (also known as **onto**) if, for *every* element $y$ in $Y,$ there is at least one element in $X$ that maps to $y.$ 

Symbolically, we can write:

$f:X\to Y$ is a surjection if $∀\,y\in Y,$ $∃\,x\in X$ such that $f(x)=y.$

With this in mind, let's check each function.

- “$f:{0,1,2}\to {1,3,9,27}$ defined by $f(x)={3}^{x}$” is *not* a surjection. As a counterexample, choose $27$ from the codomain. The only number $x$ that satisfies $f(x)={3}^{x}=27$ is $x=3,$ but $3\notin {0,1,2}.$

- “$g:[0,\infty )\to R$ defined by $g(x)={x}^{3}$” is *not* a surjection. As a counterexample, choose $-1\in R.$ There is no number $x\in [0,\infty )$ such that $g(x)=-1.$ The only number $x$ that satisfies $g(x)={x}^{3}=-1$ is $x=-1,$ but $-1\notin [0,\infty ).$

- “$h:{0,1,2}\to {-1,1,3}$ defined by $h(x)=2x-1$” is a surjection. Indeed, $h(0)=-1,$ $h(1)=1$ and $h(2)=3.$ So, for every $y\in {-1,1,3},$ there exists an element $x\in {0,1,2}$ such that $h(x)=y.$

Therefore, the correct answer is “$h:{0,1,2}\to {-1,1,3}$ defined by $h(x)=2x-1$” only.

problem:
Suppose $f(x)=x+2{e}^{2x}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
solution:
Suppose we wish to test whether the following statement is true:

$$
f(x)=O(g(x))\,\text{as}\,x\to a
$$

where $a$ is either finite or $+\infty .$ To do this, we can examine the following limit:

$$
{lim}_{x\to a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}
$$

We have the following:

- If the limit is *finite*, the statement is true.

- If the limit is *infinite*, the statement is false.

- If the limit does not exist, the test is inconclusive.

Here, we must consider the function

$$
f(x)=x+2{e}^{2x}.
$$

Now, let's consider each statement in turn.

- Statement “$f=O(x)$ as $x\to \infty $” is false. Let $g(x)=x.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{x+2{e}^{2x}}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since direct evaluation leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{\infty }{\infty },$ we can evaluate the limit using L'Hopital's rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{x+2{e}^{2x}}{x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(x+2{e}^{2x})^{′}}{(x)^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1+4{e}^{2x}}{1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }(1+4{e}^{2x}) \\  & =\infty \end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f\ne O(x)$ as $x\to \infty .$

- Statement “$f=O({e}^{2x})$ as $x\to \infty $” is true. Let $g(x)={e}^{2x}.$ Then, using L'Hopital's rule where needed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{x+2{e}^{2x}}{{e}^{2x}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }(\frac{x}{{e}^{2x}}+\frac{2{e}^{2x}}{{e}^{2x}}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{x}{{e}^{2x}}+2 \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(x)^{′}}{({e}^{2x})^{′}}+2 \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{2{e}^{2x}}+2 \\  & =0+2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f=O({e}^{2x})$ as $x\to \infty .$

- Statement “$f=O({e}^{3x})$ as $x\to \infty $” is true. Let $g(x)={e}^{3x}.$ Then, using L'Hopital's rule where needed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{x+2{e}^{2x}}{{e}^{3x}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }(\frac{x}{{e}^{3x}}+\frac{2{e}^{2x}}{{e}^{3x}}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{x}{{e}^{3x}}+{lim}_{x\to \infty }2{e}^{-x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(x)^{′}}{({e}^{3x})^{′}}+0 \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{3{e}^{3x}} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f=O({e}^{3x})$ as $x\to \infty .$

Therefore, the correct answer is “$f=O({e}^{2x})$ as $x\to \infty $”; “$f=O({e}^{3x})$ as $x\to \infty $” only.

problem:
Which of the following integrals evaluate to zero due to symmetry?

Select all that apply.
solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to $0$ due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function $f(x)=3{x}^{2}$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =3(-x)^{2} \\  & =3{x}^{2} \\  & \ne -f(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- The function $g(x)=5{x}^{3}$ is an odd function, but integral ${\int }_{-3}^{6}5{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x$ is not of the form ${\int }_{-a}^{a}g(x)\,\text{d}x$ since the upper and lower limits are not opposites. Therefore, we cannot use symmetry to simplify the integral.

- The function $h(x)=2{x}^{5}$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}h(-x) & =2(-x)^{5} \\  & =-2{x}^{5} \\  & =-h(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-9}^{9}2{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${\int }_{-9}^{9}2{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x$ only.

problem:
Consider the solution curves of the differential equation ${y}^{′}-y={x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}.$ Which of the following are stationary points of their respective solution curve?

Select all that apply.
solution:
Recall that a stationary point of $y(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $y$ such that ${y}^{′}(c)=0.$ 

First, we make ${y}^{′}$ the subject of the equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}-y={x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}\,⟹\,{y}^{′}={x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}+y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the coordinates of our points into the differential equation and calculate the value of the derivative: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{{y}^{′}|}_{(-1,-2)} & ={({x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}+y)|}_{(-1,-2)} \\  & =(-1)^{3}+3(-1)^{2}+(-2) \\  & =0\,✓ \\ {{y}^{′}|}_{(1,1)} & ={({x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}+y)|}_{(1,1)} \\  & =(1)^{3}+3(1)^{2}+(1) \\  & =5 \\  & \ne 0\,\times  \\ {{y}^{′}|}_{(1,-2)} & ={({x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}+y)|}_{(1,-2)} \\  & =(1)^{3}+3(1)^{2}+(-2) \\  & =2 \\  & \ne 0\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $(-1,-2)$ only.

problem:
The function $y=f(x)$ satisfies the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2{x}^{3}-y.
$$

Given that the point $(1,2)$ lies on the graph of $y=f(x),$ which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
solution:
First, we find the value of the first and second derivatives of the function at the given point.

To find the first derivative of $f$ at $(1,2),$ we substitute the coordinates of our point into the differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(1,2)} & ={(2{x}^{3}-y)|}_{(1,2)} \\  & =2(1)^{3}-(2) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

To find the second derivative, we first need to differentiate the equation and then substitute the coordinates of the point:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}-y) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y) \\  & =6{x}^{2}-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\  & =6{x}^{2}-(2{x}^{3}-y) \\  & =6{x}^{2}-2{x}^{3}+y \\ {\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}|}_{(1,2)} & ={(6{x}^{2}-2{x}^{3}+y)|}_{(1,2)} \\  & =6(1)^{2}-2(1)^{3}+(2) \\  & =6 \\  & >0.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine the statements in turn.

- Statement “$(1,2)$ is a stationary point of the function $f$” is true. Indeed, since 

$$
{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(1,2)}=0,
$$

 we obtain that $(1,2)$ is a stationary point of the function $f.$

- Statement “$(1,2)$ is a local maximum point of the function $f$” is false. There is a critical point at $(1,2).$ So, according to the second derivative test, since 

$$
{\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}|}_{(1,2)}>0,
$$

 we have a local minimum (not a local maximum) at that point.

- Statement “$(1,2)$ is an inflection point of the function $f$” is false. Since the second derivative is not zero, there is no inflection point at $(1,2).$

Therefore, the correct answer is “$(1,2)$ is a stationary point of the function $f$” only.

$(1,2)$ is a local maximum point of the function $f$
$(1,2)$ is an inflection point of the function $f$

$$

- the same value $(3)$ on the main diagonal,

- $1$'s on the superdiagonal,

- zeros everywhere else.

- $C$ is *not* a Jordan block since it has nonzero entries outside the main diagonal and superdiagonal:

$$

$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$B$ only."

Given a quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}Ax,$ we have the following theorem:

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative (note that positive semi-definite quadratic forms include all positive-definite quadratic forms),

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive (note that negative semi-definite quadratic forms include all negative-definite quadratic forms), and

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

With that in mind, let's examine the statements in turn.

- Statement “The eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=7$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=10$” is false. Computing the characteristic equation of $A,$ we obtain

$$

problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A={A}^{T}
$$

Equivalently, ${a}_{ij}={a}_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement “If $A$ is *any* matrix, then $A{A}^{T}$ is always symmetric” is true. Indeed, for any $m\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A{A}^{T})^{T} & =({A}^{T})^{T}{A}^{T} \\  & =A{A}^{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “The sum of two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is always symmetric” is true. Indeed, for any two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A+B)^{T} & ={A}^{T}+{B}^{T} \\  & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “The product of two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is always symmetric” is false. As a counterexample, consider the symmetric matrices 

$\,$ $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\,$ and $\,B=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.$ 

However, their product is not symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is “If $A$ is *any* matrix, then $A{A}^{T}$ is always symmetric”; “The sum of two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is always symmetric” only.

problem:
Which of the following vector fields are conservative on ${R}^{2}?$

Select all that apply.
solution:
Let $F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j$ be a vector field with domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives everywhere on $D.$ Then, we have the following theorem:

$F$ *is conservative if and only if $\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}$ everywhere on $D.$*

Note that for each of our functions, $D={R}^{2}.$ With this in mind, let's check each of the vector fields. 

- For the vector field $F,$ we have $P=x{e}^{xy}$ and $Q=y{e}^{xy}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}={x}^{2}{e}^{xy},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={y}^{2}{e}^{xy}.
$$

Since the partial derivatives are not equal, we conclude that $F$ is not conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

- For the vector field $G,$ we have $P=xy+{y}^{2}$ and $Q=xy+{x}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=x+2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=y+2x.
$$

Since the partial derivatives are not equal, we conclude that $G$ is not conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

- For the vector field $H,$ we have $P=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)$ and $Q=-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y).$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y),\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y).
$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ we conclude that $H$ is conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is $H=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)\,j$ only.

problem:
Which of the following systems of linear ODEs are decoupled?

Select all that apply.
solution:
A *decoupled system* consists of equations depending on only one variable, such as

$$
{x}_{i}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{i}{x}_{i}(t),
$$

where ${\lambda }_{i}$ is a constant. This means that we can solve each equation independently. 

In matrix form, a linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ is decoupled if $A$ is a diagonal matrix.

With this in mind, let's examine our systems.

- Systems ${x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}x(t)$ and ${x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}x(t)$ are decoupled since their corresponding matrices are diagonal.

- System ${x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t)$ is *not* decoupled because its matrix is not diagonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is ${x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}x(t)$; ${x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}x(t)$ only.

problem:

${x}^{′}(t)=A\text{ }x(t)+f(t).$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
solution:
Recall that if ${x}_{h}(t)$ satisfies a homogeneous linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution to an inhomogeneous linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t),$ then ${x}_{h}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)$ is also a solution to the same inhomogeneous system.

Additonally, the *linearity principle* for systems of linear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) states that if ${x}_{1}(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t),…,{x}_{k}(t)$ are solutions to a homogeneous linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ then any linear combination 

$$
{c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)+⋯+{c}_{k}{x}_{k}(t)
$$

with ${c}_{1},{c}_{2},…,{c}_{k}\in R$ is also a solution of the same homogeneous system. 

With that in mind, let's examine the given expression.

- Option $3\cdot {x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)$ is a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Indeed, notice that the linear combination 

$$
{x}_{h}(t)=3\cdot {x}_{1}(t)
$$

is a solution to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ according to the linearity principle. Thus, 

$$
\underbrace{3\cdot {x}_{1}(t)}_{{x}_{h}(t)}+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

is a solution to our inhomogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t).$

- Option ${x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t)+2\cdot {x}_{p}(t)$ might be *not* a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Notice that ${x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t)+2\cdot {x}_{p}(t)$ can't be written as 

$$
{x}_{h}(t)+{x}_{p}(t),
$$

where ${x}_{h}(t)$ is a solution of the homogeneous system, because of the multiplier $2$ next to the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t).$

- Option $-4\cdot {x}_{2}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)$ is a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Indeed, notice that the linear combination 

$$
{x}_{h}(t)=-4\cdot {x}_{2}(t)
$$

is a solution to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ according to the linearity principle. Thus, 

$$
\underbrace{-4\cdot {x}_{2}(t)}_{{x}_{h}(t)}+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

is a solution to our inhomogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t).$

Therefore, the correct answer is $3\cdot {x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)$; $-4\cdot {x}_{2}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)$ only.

problem:
Let $F(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)$ for $x\in R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $\pi $-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\in [0,\pi )$ to $x\in R.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
solution:
Since $f$ is the $\pi $-periodic extension of $F,$ we have 

- $f(x+\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R,$ and

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in [0,\pi ).$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement “$f(x+\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$” is true. This is exactly the definition of $\pi $-periodicity: 

$$
f(x+\pi )=f(x)
$$

for all $x\in R.$

- Statement “$f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in R$” is true. Notice that $F$ itself is $\pi $-periodic, because for any $x\in R,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x+\pi )=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(x+\pi ))=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+2\pi )=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)=F(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $F$ already satisfies the periodicity rule, the $\pi $-periodic extension agrees with $F$ everywhere, so $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in R.$

- Statement “$f(x+\frac{5\pi }{2})=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$” is false. Since $f$ is $\pi $-periodic, shifting by $2\pi $ does not change the value of $f,$ so

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x+\frac{5\pi }{2})=f((x+\frac{\pi }{2})+2\pi )=f(x+\frac{\pi }{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

But $f(x+\frac{\pi }{2})$ does not always equal $f(x).$ For example, take $x=\frac{\pi }{3}.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{2})=f(\frac{5\pi }{6})=F(\frac{5\pi }{6})=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6})=\frac{1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

while

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{3})=F(\frac{\pi }{3})=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x+\frac{5\pi }{2})\ne f(x)$ for $x=\frac{\pi }{4}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is “$f(x+\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$”; “$f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in R$” only.

|  | $1$ | $1$ | $-6$ | $0$ |

problem:
Which of the following are third-order ordinary differential equations?

Select all that apply.
solution:
A differential equation is of third-order if the largest derivative term in the equation is ${y}^{‴}.$

Keeping this in mind, let's check each given equation.

- Equation ${y}^{‴}+3x{y}^{′}=xy$ is a third-order differential equation. The highest derivative in this equation is ${y}^{‴}.$

- Equation $3{y}^{″}{y}^{′}-2xy=2{y}^{′}$ is not a third-order differential equation. The highest derivative in this equation is ${y}^{″},$ so this is a second-order differential equation.

- Equation ${x}^{3}{y}^{′}-2x={y}^{″}$ is not a third-order differential equation. The highest derivative in this equation is ${y}^{″},$ so this is a second-order differential equation.

Therefore, the correct answer is ${y}^{‴}+3x{y}^{′}=xy$ only.

problem:
Which of the following are autonomous ordinary differential equations?

Select all that apply.
solution:
An ordinary differential equation with dependent variable $y$ and independent variable $x$ is said to be autonomous if it can be written in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y),$ or equivalently, ${y}^{′}=f(y).$

With that in mind, let's check each of the differential equations:

- Equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{y}$ is an autonomous differential equation. We see that it is of the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y),$ where $f(y)={e}^{y}.$

- Equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y=0$ is an autonomous differential equation. Writing the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =f(y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)=3y.$

- Equation $2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-xy=\sqrt{x}$ is not an autonomous differential equation. If we isolate the derivative term, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-xy & =\sqrt{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2}(xy+\sqrt{x}) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{2}(xy+\sqrt{x}).$ So, it is not possible to write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{y}$; $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y=0$ only.

problem:
Which of the following systems is a first-order initial value problem?

Select all that apply.
solution:
A first-order initial value problem (or IVP) is a first-order ordinary differential equation together with an initial condition that specifies a value of the unknown function at a point in its domain. A first-order initial value problem typically takes the form

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y({x}_{0})={y}_{0},
$$

where ${x}_{0}$ and ${y}_{0}$ are constants.

With that in mind, let's check each option.

- System $2x{y}^{′}=y,\,y(0)=1$ is a first-order initial value problem. It consists of a first-order differential equation $2x{y}^{′}=y$ together with the initial condition $y(0)=1.$

- System ${y}^{′}-2xy={e}^{y}$ is not a first-order initial value problem. We have a first-order ordinary differential equation, but there is no initial condition.

- System $2x{y}^{″}={y}^{′},\,y(1)=1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=1$ is not a first-order initial value problem. It consists of a *second*-order differential equation $2x{y}^{″}={y}^{′}$ together with *two* initial conditions $y(1)=1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=1.$ This is a second-order initial value problem.

Therefore, the correct answer is $2x{y}^{′}=y,\,y(0)=1$ only.

problem:
Which of the following random variables can be modeled as a discrete uniform distribution?

Select all that apply.
solution:
We can use the discrete uniform distribution to model the outcome of a single event when the support $S$ is finite, and each $x\in S$ is equally likely.

With that in mind, let's consider each of the given random variables.

- Random variable “The number obtained when picking an integer between $1$ and $10$ at random” can be modeled as a discrete uniform distribution. There are a finite number of integers between $1$ and $10,$ and since the selection is made at random, each integer has an equal probability of being selected.

- Random variable “The number obtained when picking a real number between $1$ and $10$ at random” cannot be modeled as a discrete uniform distribution. This is because there are infinitely many real numbers between $1$ and $10,$ and so the support is not finite.

- Random variable “The color of the ball obtained when a ball from a bag containing $3$ blue and $4$ red balls is chosen at random” cannot be modeled as a discrete uniform distribution. Each outcome is not equally likely, because there is a higher probability of selecting a red ball.

Therefore, the correct answer is “The number obtained when picking an integer between $1$ and $10$ at random” only.

problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y)=⟨y,\,-x⟩$ and the points $O(0,0)$ and $A(1,1)$ in the $xy$-plane. 

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector-valued function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

This theorem implies that the line integral of a conservative vector field depends only on the value of $f$ at the initial and terminal points $A$ and $B,$ and is independent of the path between them.

With that in mind, we consider each statement in turn.

- Statement “${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=0,$ where ${C}_{1}$ is the path along the line segment $\overset{―}{OA},$ traversed from $O$ to $A.$” is true. Parameterizing the line segment, we have

$$
{r}_{1}(t)=⟨t,\,t⟩,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}⟨t,\,-t⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,1⟩\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t-t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}0\,\text{d}t \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=0,$ where ${C}_{2}$ is the path along the parabola $y={x}^{2},$ traversed from $O$ to $A.$” is false. Parameterizing the line segment, we have

$$
{r}_{2}(t)=⟨t,\,{t}^{2}⟩,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}⟨{t}^{2},\,-t⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,2t⟩\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}-2{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ is independent of path” is false. Since ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{2}$ have the same initial and terminal points, yet

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r\ne {\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r,
$$

we conclude that ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ is path-dependent.

- Statement “$F$ is conservative” is false. If a vector field is conservative then it is path-independent. Since $F$ is path-dependent, it is not conservative.

fields.key: ${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=0,$ where ${C}_{1}$ is the path along the line segment $\overset{―}{OA},$ traversed from $O$ to $A.$
${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=0,$ where ${C}_{2}$ is the path along the parabola $y={x}^{2},$ traversed from $O$ to $A.$

problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y)=⟨{e}^{x+y},\,{e}^{x+y}⟩$ and the points $O(0,0)$ and $A(1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)$ in the $xy$-plane. 

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector-valued function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

This theorem implies that the line integral of a conservative vector field depends only on the value of $f$ at the initial and terminal points $A$ and $B,$ and is independent of the path between them.

With that in mind, we consider each statement in turn.

- Statement “$F$ is conservative” is true. Notice that $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ with domain $D={R}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={e}^{x+y}.
$$

Since the partial derivatives exist and are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ we conclude that $F$ is conservative.

- Statement “${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=2e-1,$ where ${C}_{1}$ is the path along the line segment $\overset{―}{OA},$ traversed from $O$ to $A.$” is true. Since $F$ is conservative, there exists a function $f$ such that $∇f=F.$ Reconstructing the function $f$ from its gradient in the usual way, we get

$$
f={e}^{x+y}.
$$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}∇f\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =f(1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)-f(0,0) \\  & ={e}^{1+\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-{e}^{0} \\  & =e\cdot {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-1 \\  & =2e-1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=2e-1,$ where ${C}_{2}$ is the path along the curve $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1),$ traversed from $O$ to $A.$” is true. Since $F$ is conservative and ${C}_{2}$ has the same initial and terminal points as ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=2e-1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is “$F$ is conservative”; “${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=2e-1,$ where ${C}_{1}$ is the path along the line segment $\overset{―}{OA},$ traversed from $O$ to $A.$”; “${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=2e-1,$ where ${C}_{2}$ is the path along the curve $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1),$ traversed from $O$ to $A.$”.

fields.key: ${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=2e-1,$ where ${C}_{1}$ is the path along the line segment $\overset{―}{OA},$ traversed from $O$ to $A.$
${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=2e-1,$ where ${C}_{2}$ is the path along the curve $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1),$ traversed from $O$ to $A.$

- Equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{y}{x+1}$ does *not* give the required behavior. The right-hand side of ${y}^{′}=\frac{y}{x+1}$ evaluates to zero on $y=0,$ but

$$

$$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${y}^{′}=\frac{y}{x-1}$ only.

Which of the following random variables could be modeled by an exponential distribution?

solution:
The exponential distribution can be thought of as the continuous analog of the geometric distribution. It models the amount of continuous time or space until a particular event occurs, where the events should occur independently and at a constant average rate.

With that in mind, let's consider each of the given random variables.

- Random variable “The amount of time until the next earthquake in a particular country” could be modeled using an exponential distribution. Earthquakes can be modeled as independent events with a constant average rate, and we wish to know the amount of time until the next earthquake occurs.

- Random variable “The number of giraffes in a zoo” does *not* follow an exponential distribution. There are no events that occur at a constant average rate, and there is no interval of continuous time or space.

- Random variable “The number of defective bottles produced in a factory in a single day” does *not* follow an exponential distribution. There is no interval of continuous time or space. The number of defective bottles produced is discrete, not continuous.

$$
\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=0
$$

and, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T) & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =2-0 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement “$\text{rank}(T)=1$,  where $T$ is the standard matrix of $T$” is false. In our case, we have 

$$

$$

- Statement “$\text{Im}(T)$ contains no vectors of ${R}^{2}$” is false. The image of $T$ contains the vector zero vector $0=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

- Statement $\text{Ker}(T)={R}^{2}$ is true. Indeed, the condition $\text{nullity}(T)=2$ in ${R}^{2}$ is equivalent to 

$$
\text{Ker}(T)={R}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $\text{Ker}(T)={R}^{2}$ only.

problem:
Suppose that $f(x)$ is defined as

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}x-1, & x<0.5 \\ 4-{x}^{2}, & x\ge 0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

On which of the following intervals can the extreme value theorem be applied to the function?

Select all that apply.
solution:
Remember that the extreme value theorem is only applicable to closed intervals on which the function is continuous.

So, let's check whether the function is continuous on each of the intervals.

- The interval $(0,1)$ is not closed, so the extreme value theorem is not applicable.

- Now, consider $[0,2].$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0.5}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to 0.5}(x-1)=(0.5)-1=-0.5, \\ {lim}_{x\to {0.5}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to 0.5}(4-{x}^{2})=4-(0.5)^{2}=3.75.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the limits from the left and from the right of $x=0.5$ are not the same. Hence, $f(x)$ has a discontinuity at $x=0.5.$ Therefore, $f(x)$ is not continuous on the interval $[0,2],$ and the extreme value theorem is not applicable on this interval.

- Finally, consider $[1,2].$ The only discontinuity of the function $f(x)$ is at $x=0.5,$ which is not in the interval $[1,2].$ Therefore, $f(x)$ is continuous on the interval $[1,2],$ and the extreme value theorem is applicable on this interval.

In conclusion, the correct answer is $[1,2]$ only.

- Statement “The series diverges at $x=2$” is false. Since $2\notin [-1,2),$ we cannot guarantee that the series is divergent at $x=2.$

problem:
Consider the affine transformation $T$ defined as

$$
x=v-u,\,y=u+v-1.
$$

Let $A$ be the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T.$

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's look at each statement in turn:

- Statement $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ is false. Notice that the given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}v-u \\ u+v-1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-u+v \\ u+v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{A}\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{u}+\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.$

- Statement $det(A)=-2$ is true. Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}=1\cdot (-1)-1\cdot 1=-2.
$$

- Statement “The transformation $T$ is orientation-preserving” is false. Since $det(A)<0,$ the affine transformation $T$ is not orientation-preserving.

Therefore, the correct answer is $det(A)=-2$ only.

$$

$$

$$

Let $A$ be the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T.$

An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's look at each statement in turn:

- Statement $A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}$ is false. Notice that the given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3u-v+2 \\ v-u\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3u-v \\ -u+v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{A}\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{u}+\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is $A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.$

- Statement $det(A)=-2$ is false. Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{vmatrix}=3\cdot 1-(-1)\cdot (-1)=2.
$$

If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

To understand the flux intuitively, we imagine that $F$ represents a stream of flowing water. The flux of $F$ across $C$ represents the net flow of water escaping the region bounded by $C:$ 

- If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*.

- If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*.

![](images/a7/a72dc9866562a42a49590fd169424307675b2c14b36833bd729026f46b677eec.png)

- If the net flow through $C$ is zero then the flux equals zero.

![](images/3a/3a6ac8656b2e0b5cc482a16eb3a4fab57cb681c9a40cf634da47f9a4323d9fdf.png)

For an arbitrary closed curve, the outward-pointing unit normal vector tells us which direction is "out."

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement “The flux of $F$ across $C$ is positive” is true, while statement “The flux of $F$ across $C$ is zero” is false. From the diagram below it's clear that there is a net flow *out* through $C.$ 

![](images/fb/fbcd6fd0fadcc955212a145de9edb4654ddb92ddebb8ba31eb775cff676efeeb.png)

Therefore, the flux is positive, and we must have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s>0.
$$

- Statement “The flux of $F$ across $-C$ is positive” is true. When measuring flux through a closed curve, the orientation of the curve does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same at each point on $C$ in either case.

![](images/a3/a3d398d382e6bc94ddde77e650d50a6b5ec050083f89f64104f6f2fd172a9239.png)

So, the flux of $F$ across $-C$ is positive, and we must have

$$
{∮}_{-C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s>0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is “The flux of $F$ across $C$ is positive”; “The flux of $F$ across $-C$ is positive” only.
